messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marco is a twenty-two-year-old HVAC technician living in a small apartment in Phoenix. Eight months ago, while working on a rooftop unit at a strip mall, he misjudged a pressure valve on an aging refrigerant line. The line burst, and a shard of metal struck a fellow technician in the neck. The man survived but suffered a spinal injury that left him partially paralyzed. Marco remembers the jet of gas, the smell of compressor oil and ozone, the way the other man’s eyes went wide before he crumpled. The image comes back without warning—sometimes when he’s driving, sometimes in the middle of a quiet job—and when it does, he can smell that oil again, sharp and chemical, as if it’s right there in the air. But the memory doesn’t feel like his own. He has described it to his therapist as watching a scene from a movie, or something that happened to someone else, even though he knows it was his hands on that valve.

Marco has come to believe that his body is fundamentally unreliable. He can no longer trust his reflexes, his judgment, his own hands. The thought that he could have done something different—could have checked the gauge one more time, could have yelled a warning—echoes through his mind daily, and he is certain he will never forgive himself for not stopping what happened. That guilt drives him to replay the event over and over, analyzing each second for where he went wrong, as though he might find a version of the past in which he did enough. In the weeks after the accident he stopped going out with friends, stopped answering calls from his supervisor, and began timing his work schedule to avoid any job that reminded him of that rooftop. He refuses to accept assignments that involve refrigeration lines, even though that means lost income and tense conversations with his boss. The anniversaries—the date of the accident, the date the other man was discharged from the hospital—loom like deadlines he cannot escape, and he dreads them months in advance.

What frightens Marco most is silence. Unusual quiet—an empty parking lot, a lunch break in a dead hallway—makes him feel that something dangerous is about to happen. His body reacts before his mind can catch up: his heart pounds, his palms sweat, and he has to leave. As a result, he has shrunk his world to a few places where he feels safe: his apartment with the television always on, his cousin’s garage, one specific aisle of a grocery store where the background noise is constant. He is aware that this is unsustainable, but the moment he steps into a quieter space, the intrusive memory of the accident rises again—the hiss of the valve, the silence that followed before the other man screamed—and the threat feeling spikes. The memory and the threat feed each other; the more he avoids, the fewer places feel safe, and the more the memory forces its way in during the rare moments of quiet he cannot control.

Marco’s avoidance and overanalyzing have only deepened his sense that he is no longer the person he used to be. He used to be easygoing, quick to laugh, confident in his work. Now he cannot trust himself to do a simple repair without checking and rechecking. Each time he avoids a stressor—a job site, a social invitation—he tells himself he did the right thing, but underneath there is a quiet voice that says, *See? You can’t be trusted around anyone.* That self-appraisal tightens the loop, and the urge to ruminate grows stronger. He has stopped seeing his family because they ask how he is doing, and the question brings the memory back with its alien quality, as though the accident belongs to a stranger whose life he is now living.

He sought help after his supervisor gave him a final warning about missed assignments. Marco sat in the quiet of his apartment, the television off for once, and felt the familiar dread creep in. He realized he had not left that apartment in four days, and that the person he had become was someone he barely recognized. What he hopes for—though he can barely admit it—is to feel that his own body is his again, and to find a way to live with what his hands did without letting it consume everything else.
